title: Fatigue Management Pattern
body: DT-128 put a fully loaded truck into the Stage 6 high wall because the operator was asleep at the wheel 405 meters into the haul — road and berms were to design, the roster wasn't. When fatigue only gets caught at the point of a near-miss or a strike, you've already lost the chance to stop it.
keyPoints: The roster is the root cause until proven otherwise. DT-128's 13-on, 12-hour, 24-off pattern was judged unmanageable for fatigue — and it echoes DT-77 from January 2024, where the fix stopped at blaming the operator instead of the roster. Don't let a fatigue incident close as an individual failing if the schedule put them there.
12 hours is the hard cap, full stop. No operator works beyond it, and rotation overstays (crews running 5-7 months instead of 1-2) get HOD-arranged relief, not silence.
Self-reporting only works if people trust it. Operators are staying quiet because they fear losing their job or badge over a Fatigue Form. A form nobody trusts isn't a control — it's paperwork.

Watch the reporting gap, not just the count. September logged 16 clinic visits against 1 fatigue report, and Production logged 43 fatigue events to Workshop's 5 year-to-date. That gap is a flag that people are quietly absorbing fatigue as rest time instead of documenting it.
apply: If you're giving someone rest time off the books because they look worn down, log it on the Fatigue Form anyway — the trend data is only as good as what actually gets reported, and right now it's underselling the real picture.
